user.title: ADS-B station
user.description: What runs on your receiver? Anything that serves an aircraft.json works: dump1090, dump1090-fa and SkyAware, readsb and tar1090. Add the Flightradar24 feeder on top only if you actually run fr24feed.

fr24feed.title: Flightradar24 feeder
fr24feed.description: Enter the address of your Flightradar24 feeder. Home Assistant reads the status page that fr24feed serves on your own receiver.

data_description.host: The IP address or hostname of the device running fr24feed, for example 192.168.5.7.

piaware.description: Enter the address of the machine running PiAware. The port is the one its status page is served on, 8080 by default.

data_description.port: The port serving status.json. FlightAware's own tooling uses 8080; a station whose web server was taken over by something else may serve it elsewhere.

data_description.port: The port of the pfclient web interface. The default is 30053.

receiver.title: ADS-B receiver
receiver.description: Enter the address of the machine running your decoder. Home Assistant looks for its aircraft.json in the usual places.

data_description.host: The IP address or hostname of the device running the decoder, for example 192.168.5.7.

aircraft.title: ADS-B receiver
aircraft.description: Home Assistant can also read the aircraft.json of your decoder for the number of aircraft received, the message rate and the maximum range. Leave the field empty to skip this. Leave it empty if another entry on this station already reads the decoder, or its aircraft will be counted twice.

data_description.aircraft_url: The full URL to aircraft.json, for example http://192.168.5.7:8080/dump1090/data/aircraft.json. Detected automatically when possible.
data_description.units: What heights, speeds and distances are given in, on the sensors, in their attributes and events, by voice and on the card, and what you fill in: the radius and the ceiling under Configure, and the filters of the actions. As Home Assistant follows its own unit system: metric, or imperial for its US units. Aviation is feet, knots and nautical miles.

receiver_url.title: aircraft.json
receiver_url.description: This is where the data comes from, so it is required. Any decoder that serves an aircraft.json works, whichever network you feed.

data_description.aircraft_url: The full URL to aircraft.json, for example http://192.168.5.7/tar1090/data/aircraft.json. Detected automatically when possible.
data_description.units: What heights, speeds and distances are given in, on the sensors, in their attributes and events, by voice and on the card, and what you fill in: the radius and the ceiling under Configure, and the filters of the actions. As Home Assistant follows its own unit system: metric, or imperial for its US units. Aviation is feet, knots and nautical miles.

data.follow_units: Let sensors with a unit of their own follow

data_description.scan_interval: How often the aircraft are read, in seconds. Everything runs on your own network, so a short interval is fine.
data_description.statistics_interval: How often the feeder and the decoder's statistics are read, in seconds. Those are counters and averages over a minute, so reading them more often mostly fills the recorder. A station that only feeds is read at this interval alone.
data_description.proximity_radius: How close an aircraft has to be to count as nearby, in the unit shown beside it. Ten kilometres, about six miles, is roughly what you can see and hear.
data_description.proximity_max_altitude: How high an aircraft may be and still count as nearby, in the unit shown beside it. Leave it empty and the radius alone decides, which is worth knowing about: a radius is a circle on the ground, so without a ceiling an airliner at 36,000 feet is overhead. It applies to what is nearby, what is overhead and what counts as a passage, and to nothing else: the aircraft still counts as received, still sets range records, and an emergency squawk is still reported at any height.
data_description.keep_passages: How many days the passages are kept after the board on Passages today starts over at midnight, to look them up with the List passages action. 0 keeps none. They are kept in a file of their own under .storage, about 200 bytes a passage, written at most every quarter of an hour.
data_description.map_aircraft: Puts every aircraft inside the nearby radius on the map as its own entity, for as long as it is there. Nothing is registered and nothing is kept, so they leave no trace once they have flown on; that also means they cannot be renamed or hidden individually, and they are not listed under this station's device.
data_description.look_up_routes: No aircraft broadcasts where it is flying from or to, so this has to be asked of a service on the internet. It uses routeset, the same source tar1090 does. Only the aircraft inside the nearby radius are looked up, and answers are kept for the day.
data_description.look_up_photos: Adds a photo of each aircraft inside the nearby radius, and of each one on the watchlist, from Planespotters.net. Only the address the aircraft broadcasts is sent, and answers are kept for a day. The photos are lent on condition that the photographer is named beside one and that it links to its page, so they come as attributes for a dashboard card rather than as entity pictures.
data_description.watchlist: Aircraft worth knowing about whenever they turn up, one to a line. There is no radius: this asks whether the aircraft is in the air at all, however far away. A line can be a hex code (484123), a registration or a callsign (PH-BXA, KLM123), an aircraft type (EC35), a squawk (7700), the start of a registration or callsign (PH-B*, KLM*), military, helicopter or a country (country:US).
data_description.aircraft_database: Your decoder names no aircraft itself, so registrations and types are missing. This downloads the tar1090-db table (Mictronics' data, about 9 MB) straight from GitHub to your Home Assistant at most once a week, keeps it on disk, about 26 MB, and looks the aircraft you hear up there. Nothing about them leaves your network. Switching it off deletes the file.
data_description.units: What heights, speeds and distances are given in, on the sensors, in their attributes and events, by voice and on the card, and what you fill in: the radius and the ceiling here, and the filters of the actions. As Home Assistant follows its own unit system: metric, or imperial for its US units. Aviation is feet, knots and nautical miles.

error.unreadable_watchlist: These lines are not a hex code, a registration or callsign, an aircraft type, a squawk or a group such as KLM*, military or country:US: {lines}

receiver_silent.title: {station} hears nothing
receiver_silent.description:
The dongle of {station} has delivered nothing to the decoder for {minutes} minutes. A working dongle hands over millions of samples a second, whether or not anything is flying, so this is the dongle and not a quiet sky: it dropped off the USB bus, or it did not come back after a reboot because it never lost power.

Unplug the dongle and plug it back in, or restart the decoder. This message goes away by itself as soon as the dongle delivers again.

bad_tuner.title: The dongle of {station} has a tuner that hears 1090 MHz badly
bad_tuner.description:
readsb reports that the dongle of {station} has an FC0012, FC0013 or FC2580 tuner. Those come from cheap TV sticks and receive 1090 MHz badly, so the station hears far fewer aircraft, and far less far, than it could. Nothing is broken; it is the wrong kind of dongle.

Use a dongle made for ADS-B, or one with an R820T, R828D or R860 tuner. This message goes away by itself once readsb no longer reports it.

confirm.title: Units of {station}
confirm.description:
Since 1.4, {station} gives heights, speeds and distances in the units chosen here, everywhere: the sensors, their attributes, the events, the actions, Activity, Assist and the card. They are now {units}; before, heights were in feet, speeds in knots and distances in kilometres.

Numbers you wrote yourself are read in these units too: an automation comparing a height, speed or distance, and the card's map_range and max_altitude. Nothing can convert those for you, so look them over, or pick Aviation to keep heights in feet and speeds in knots, with distances in nautical miles.

look_up_aircraft.name: Look up aircraft
look_up_aircraft.description: Answers with everything this station knows about one aircraft, by hex code or callsign, out of its last poll.

aircraft.name: Aircraft
aircraft.description: The hex code or the callsign, in either case. An aircraft this station is not hearing answers with nothing, which is not an error.

config_entry.name: Station
config_entry.description: Which station to ask. Only needed when more than one of your entries carries a receiver.

list_passages.name: List passages
list_passages.description: Answers with the passages this station has kept that match, most recent first. How many days are kept is set under Configure.

aircraft.name: Aircraft
aircraft.description: A hex code, callsign or registration. Leave it empty for every aircraft.

start.name: From
start.description: Only passages that began at or after this moment.

end.name: Until
end.description: Only passages that began at or before this moment.

config_entry.name: Station
config_entry.description: Which station to ask. Only needed when more than one of your entries carries a receiver.

list_aircraft.name: List aircraft
list_aircraft.description: Answers with every aircraft this station is hearing that matches, nearest first. Without a single filter that is everything the decoder is holding, which reaches far beyond the nearby radius.

max_distance.name: Within
max_distance.description: How far out to look, in the station's units. Aircraft that never sent a position are left out, because there is no telling how far away they are.

min_altitude.name: Higher than
min_altitude.description: In the station's units. Aircraft that report no altitude are left out.

max_altitude.name: Lower than
max_altitude.description: In the station's units. Aircraft that report no altitude are left out.

military.name: Military
military.description: On for military traffic only, off for everything but.

category.name: Category
category.description: The emitter category an aircraft broadcasts, A0 to D7. A7 is a helicopter and B6 a drone.

config_entry.name: Station
config_entry.description: Which station to ask. Only needed when more than one of your entries carries a receiver.

install_sentences.name: Install voice sentences
install_sentences.description: Copies the spoken sentences this integration ships into your configuration directory, where Assist reads them from. Only an administrator can run it. Run conversation.reload afterwards, or restart.

speak.name: Speak an answer
speak.description: Returns one of the six spoken answers as text, ready for a sentence trigger to say back. Needs no sentence files.

question.name: Question
question.description: Which of the six to answer: what is overhead, how many are up there, which is closest, whether a kind of traffic is in range, where the aircraft overhead is going, or what came over last.

kind.name: Kind
kind.description: For the traffic question only: military, helicopter or drone.

language.name: Language
language.description: Which language to answer in. Defaults to the language of your Home Assistant; English and Dutch are spoken, anything else is answered in English.

config_entry.name: Station
config_entry.description: Which station to ask. Only needed when more than one of your entries carries a receiver.

watch.name: Watch for an aircraft
watch.description: Puts one line on the watchlist of a station, as if it were added under Configure. It is watched for from the next poll.

aircraft.name: Aircraft
aircraft.description: A hex code (484123), a registration or callsign (PH-BXA, KLM123), an aircraft type (EC35) or a squawk (7700). A line already on the list is left as it is.

config_entry.name: Station
config_entry.description: Whose watchlist to change. Only needed when more than one of your entries carries a receiver.

unwatch.name: Stop watching for an aircraft
unwatch.description: Takes one line off the watchlist of a station, however it was written there.

aircraft.name: Aircraft
aircraft.description: The line to take off: PH-BXA takes off PHBXA as well.

config_entry.name: Station
config_entry.description: Whose watchlist to change. Only needed when more than one of your entries carries a receiver.
